vignette: She sits across from me, hands resting on the worn leather armrests, but her eyes are tracking the dust motes dancing in the afternoon sun. At seventy, she carries the geometry of a photographer: she notices light, she measures distance, she knows exactly where to place herself to avoid being caught in the wrong frame. That training exists in the cramped flat where the walls close in at dusk. Her mother’s belt is not a tool of discipline but a sudden weather system. She learns to read the creak of the linoleum, the heavy thud of the key in the lock, the way the air shifts when the caregiver comes through the door. When the violence begins, she stops making noise. She curls into the corner of her bed, pulling a thread from her sweater until her fingers bleed, memorizing the exact spot on the wall that stays out of reach. She tells herself that if she becomes small enough, she will cease to exist to her. She survives. She leaves the flat, outlives a marriage that dissolves under the weight of unsaid apologies, and learns to speak through a viewfinder instead of her own voice. Today, her studio is a sanctuary of controlled exposure. She still shoots film. She prefers the chemical darkroom, the slow reveal, the way an image takes time to surface. When she hangs large-scale portraits on her studio walls, she adjusts the tension on each wire until it is perfectly level. Her hands tremble only when someone raises a voice above a conversational tone. Last week, a delivery driver dropped a box of archival paper. The sharp crack echoes through the gallery space. She drops her coffee cup, heart hammering against her ribs, and finds herself pressed against the back of the darkroom door, counting the seconds until the sound passes. She tells the driver, who is apologizing profusely, that it is fine. She waits until his footsteps fade before she allows herself to exhale. She does not sleep. Sleep, she says, is just the mind’s way of leaving the lock off. She keeps her bedroom door propped open with a wooden chair, not because she fears the dark, but because she fears the silence that follows the creak of old floorboards. When the house settles, she wakes instantly, muscles locked, scanning the room for the angle of threat. She has stopped attending family gatherings at the community center. The clatter of steel tiffins, the sudden laughter that rises too quickly, the way men in the room shift their weight in their chairs—it all triggers a familiar freeze. She tells herself she is too tired, but the truth is heavier. She no longer trusts her own nervous system to distinguish between memory and now. She works alone now. Her photographs have always been quiet subjects: abandoned balconies in the old quarter, monsoon puddles reflecting cracked tile, the slow oxidation of brass fixtures. She avoids faces. When she does shoot people, she uses a long lens and remains behind her camera, letting the glass be both shield and interpreter. She drinks chai at exactly eight and four, sets her keys in the same ceramic bowl, walks the same three blocks every evening. Routine is not a comfort; it is a structural beam holding up a collapsing ceiling. Yesterday, she showed me a contact sheet from a recent shoot. The frames are nearly identical, each one slightly out of focus, as if she is afraid to commit to a single moment. “I keep waiting for the light to change,” she says, tracing a blank strip of film with her thumb. “But it never does.” Her voice does not shake. It simply holds a flat, practiced calm, the kind that comes from years of swallowing words before they can be heard. She watches me watch her, measuring the distance between our chairs, calculating the time it would take to cross the room if she needs to. She does not look away. She has never learned how.
